utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since we have resolved the technical problems, as far as I understand, we can now concentrate again on the facts and on the legal issues. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I was informed that you would like to address the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Mr. President. Good morning to all of you. The reason that we wanted to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness is as follows: Here, on my left-hand side, I have, by way of example, just only one binder, which I lift here with some difficulty because of its weight. It is a binder which we received from the Prosecution, and it contains a considerable number of documents whose nature is strictly military. The documents originate from the so-called Bosniak army, that is, the army of Sarajevo, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have received about five binders of this size. I don't want to show them all to you. I think you can see it from your distance. All of these binders are exclusively written in the Serbian language, in its Bosnian version. Thank you for the interpretation. The problem we're faced with is the following: These documents have not been translated into one or the other working languages of the Tribunal, that is, neither in the language of Shakespeare or in the language of Voltaire. Consequently, it is not possible for the teams to examine, in a rapid fashion, the contents of these binders. Mr. President, the reason I'm raising the issue now is because in Geneva, we have people who work in my rear base, if I may call it that way, and it is not possible for them to read all of these documents because they're very time-consuming, and we cannot do it properly in view of the significance of our task. We will produce shortly some of the documents which I believe will clarify the problem, but the Defence is sure that there are other documents as well, and we just wanted to draw your attention to this particular problem, which is only an example. And speaking of Article -- that is, of Rule 90(H)(ii), I have to say that it is not always possible to present evidence simply because the evidence has not been presented to us in either of the working languages of the Tribunal. There is another reason why I'm raising this issue. Three weeks ago we had a meeting with the Prosecution, and we made an urgent request to be able to obtain from the Prosecution other military documents that they have, in particular, maps originating from the general staff, from the headquarters, military instructions, military orders which were allegedly given by various military formations or specific brigades and other such units. To this date, Mr. President, we have not received such documents, in any language, which means -- and I make note of that. The Defence makes note of that and I personally wish to make note of that -- that we, in view of such circumstances and in these conditions, we cannot protect the rights of the accused in a proper manner. We believe that this constitutes a violation of one of the fundamental principles of justice, that is, the right to fair and expeditious trial. This is just to indicate what difficulties the Defence is facing at the moment. We managed to find several pieces of evidence within these binders that we requested translation of, so we called the Prosecution at about 2100 hours, but we didn't find anyone, so we simply propose to have unofficial translation, that is, we supplied the booths with the relevant document; however, if these documents should be tendered later on in the proceedings as exhibits, we would like to make mention of the fact that we were forced to translate these documents overnight, very urgently, and that is the reason that we might have certain purely translation problems. This is an extremely important issue, Mr. President, because, as you will be able to see shortly -- and I can tell you right away in order to be loyal -- these documents prove the existence of four or five checkpoints in the squares that we have mentioned during the proceedings. It is possible that we will have a written translation soon, and the fact that these translations have not gone through the appropriate services of the Tribunal has to do with the obvious lack of organisation, that is, that we were not able to organise this. And this is mainly the reason why I'm raising this as a problem. Having said that, we are ready to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness; however, with the caveat that I have just exposed. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there -- would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would, Mr. President. Mr. Piletta-Zanin has not identified the documents as being documents provided pursuant to the reciprocal disclosure requirements or documents which are on the exhibit list. That is a very important distinction. If they are documents which we have provided pursuant to Rule 66, that is, pursuant to our obligations under reciprocal disclosure, then he can have no complaint against the Prosecution. Rule 66(B) simply requires the Prosecutor to permit the Defence to inspect the relevant documents. The Prosecution has gone one step further and chosen to provide the Defence with copies of the documents which they seek. It is certainly not incumbent upon the Prosecution to translate the documents it has in its possession which fall within the ambit of Rule 66. The Prosecution has the same difficulty as the Defence. If we had a translation, then we would provide it under Rule 66, although we are not required to do that. Secondly, my friend refers to what he calls an urgent request made three weeks ago. That request was for certain orders from the ABiH. We have provided such orders. The request from the Defence dates back many months, and I have informed the Defence that if we come across any other orders which fall within the ambit of Rule 66, then we would provide them. My friend complains that he was unable to contact us at 9.00 p.m. I assume he means 9.00 p.m. last night. I don't know if we could be expected to be here at 9.00 p.m. without any prior notice from the Defence. I am grateful that my friend is complying with Rule 90(H)(ii), and of course we will do all that we reasonably can to assist in the relevant material being placed before Prosecution witnesses in cross-examination. If he has documents which he wishes to put before the witness today, then certainly the Prosecution has no difficulty with copies of those documents being made available to the interpreters so that we can all have, in effect, an on-the-spot translation. Thank you. I should add, Mr. President, that whilst the Prosecution naturally maintains that the Rules of the Tribunal should be complied with, that applies in respect of Rule 90(H)(ii), in my view, in relation to instructions which the Defence has at the time that the witness gives his or her evidence and the material which the Defence has, and where the incidents in the witness's evidence are contained in statements which have been disclosed to the Defence prior to the giving the evidence, then clearly, prima facie, the Defence has had an opportunity to seek instructions. And when the events, such as a bombardment of the city of Sarajevo for some six hours, or the firing of tanks, five tanks, for 20 minutes, is the nature of that evidence, then one assumes that there would be no difficulty in obtaining instructions from the accused in relation to those incidents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask a few questions to start with. The binders you're talking about, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, when did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would have to check the date. I cannot tell you at this point. It must have been either in October or in November last year, but off the top of my head, I cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, do I understand that these binders we are talking about are not exhibits you'd intend to use during the examination of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if -- they haven't been clearly identified by my friend, but I assume they are ABiH documents which were disclosed to the Defence on the 23rd of October, 2001, pursuant to our reciprocal disclosure obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I ask you another question. Have you got any idea on how -- since when these documents were in your possession, or was it because of the reciprocal obligations you, well, more or less brought into by the Defence? Could you give us any idea on why it was in October that you disclosed these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll check the date, Mr. President, and come back to you. I don't know off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do I understand you well that you say we identified certain documents we'd like to use during the cross-examination in these binders, and that you're not able to have them translated officially?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. You have seen one binder. There are five or six binders of this kind. These are the binders that contain technical documents. There is a number of abbreviations, and it is very difficult to read these documents even in Serbian, so we obviously need translations. Let me also mention that we have not received the documents that have been indicated and which are connected with the 1st Army Corps, the BH army. These documents are extremely important and are of a vital significance for the Defence, and we have been waiting for them even before the month of October 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you seek leave to have them translated on the spot while using them during the cross-examination? Apart from the other problems you have with the documents, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I think that it would be much wiser when it comes to these documents that they be translated officially. I think that it is one of the rights of the accused here to have this done for him, and also for your benefit. If these documents should be tendered to you, they have to be properly translated, especially in view of the fact that they are very technical in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please indicate where in the Rules you find a basis for your submission that documents disclosed to you on the basis of a reciprocal disclosure obligation should be translated when they have been given to you, or is it just the general fairness of the trial you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It is a general principle related to the conduct of the proceedings, and not only the application of some specific provision. However, I may invoke in this context Articles 20 and 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Well, it's clear to the Chamber what your submission is, that they should have been translated anyhow and that at least, since they're not translated at this moment, you seek at least leave to have them translated, and you take the position that they should be translated officially anyhow if the Chamber would like to -- if they are presented to the Chamber. I'd like to draw your attention at least to extensive case law of this Tribunal as far as translations are concerned, and the basic rule is that all of the documents that have been presented and accompanying the indictments, that they should at least be translated. But there is a variety of case law on what other documents should be translated. I think your submission is quite clear to us at this moment. We do see the difficulties you are facing. I would suggest that we bring in the witness and we'll see whether -- when you want to give any documents to the witness and what to do with it, whether they will be tendered into evidence or not. Mr. Usher, would you then please -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we bring in the witnesses into the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before the witness comes in, could Mr. Ierace answer the question relating to the black boxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that that's what he indicated yesterday, that he would find out about the photographs which are referred to as black boxes, and that he would inform you. I do understand from your observation that the black boxes have not been opened yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm surprised to hear that question. I showed Mr. Piletta-Zanin, at the first break after he raised the issue, the photographs and explained to him that the problem was that they had been electronically copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's why they came out black. And that they would provide him with proper copies of the photographs. He then said to me that his real concern was another issue to do with the document. That issue was that there was mention on the first page ever there being two places where incidents had taken place, and he wanted that clarified. And I've been making some inquiries about that. So I say formally now for the benefit of the Trial Chamber that I've shown the photographs to my friend, and we will provide proper copies of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. There seems to be a very serious misunderstanding here. I saw the originals of these photographs, and we have relatively clear copies of these photographs. However, as regards the incidents on the square, the Rade Koncara square and the other one, Zavnobih Square, concern -- these incidents involve two projectiles, two shells. However, the photos which were shown on two occasions, 430 and 431, it seems they relate only to one of these squares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... dealt with during cross-examination once they have been tendered into evidence. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace, any additional observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I hesitate to prolong this debate, because Mr. Kucanin is anxious to get away, but according to my transcript, Mr. Piletta-Zanin has just admitted that he has relatively clear copies of those photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Which begs the question: Why is he complaining about a version of the photographs which came out black? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think everything that has to be said during this debate has been said by now. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Merely for the booths. I use the word "objective" and it was translated as "headquarters." When I say "objective," then the interpretation should be "target." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that this remark will be worked in the transcript when it will be redacted during the late evening hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kucanin. Should I say "dobar dan."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also did hear me in the other language in the translation. Yes. Mr. Kucanin, you still had to wait for another half an hour, due partly to technical problems, partly to legal problems we had to discuss. Mr. Piletta-Zanin will now continue the cross-examination. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you made the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Thank you for returning to this courtroom. I'd like to resume from where we stopped, more or less, yesterday. You said in your statement, in your evidence before this Chamber, speaking about two squares, that it could be that a civilian in a uniform had passed -- had crossed them. I'm quoting it from yesterday's transcript, and a question which I asked about the presence of uniformed individuals, and I believe that your answer was that there was nobody wearing a uniform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see anyone wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how can you explain what you said before this Chamber, that you had seen, and I'm quoting you, civilians in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd be grateful if my friend could indicate the page where the witness said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have already said. It was 10:56:12. We had a non-edited transcript, so this is the only indication that I have. And I am quoting from yesterday's text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- since I have difficulties finding it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please quote literally so that we have the exact wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so, Mr. President, but I believe, speaking from memory, that the text was [In English], "A citizen in uniform may have passed by." [Interpretation] [In English], "A citizen in uniform may have passed by."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've just done a quick search on the word "uniform," and the first apparently relevant entry that comes up is page 81, line 9, where Mr. Piletta-Zanin said in cross-examination to this witness -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exact quotation, I've found it, and the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would -- you found the line, so if you read it literally, then -- I have difficulty, since I have the other numbering of the pages, so I'm somewhere in 4,000 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm very sorry about these problems. We were working on the text which we had at the time. And the day before yesterday -- sorry, the 10:05:16, the answer was the following, and I'm quoting: "[In English] A citizen [Interpretation] and I repeat for the booths: [Previous translation continues]... [In English] In uniform may have passed by, but there was no military formation there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please also repeat the question preceding, or don't you have it at this very moment? It is my recollection that the witness left open the possibility that a civilian in uniform or whatever person wearing a uniform might have passed by, but that he did not see any military formation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. That is what I just quoted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Now that my friend has identified it as the day before yesterday, I have the passage. On my copy it's page 4521, that's page 4521, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that. 4,000 you said and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find it. 4521.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the question begins at line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the page by now. I'll read it. The question was: "Did you notice any soldiers in the vicinity when you arrived?" The answer was: "I didn't notice any particular formation. A citizen in uniform may have passed by, but there was no military formation there. Later on I learned, but the name escapes me at the moment, but nothing that would indicate that there was any military presence in the area, no, nothing." That was the literal wording of what I find in the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is precisely it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And we are coming back to this point now, Witness. But briefly, when you speak about a citizen in a uniform, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been a postman. Will you ask me a specific question if you want a specific answer from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So it could have been a postman, it could have been a station master, it could have been a policeman, and it could have been a soldier; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just first clarify. Mr. Kucanin, did you tell the Court that you saw a civilian that passed by, or did you tell the Court that there might have been a civilian passing by, but you were not aware of any military formation? I mean, did you see someone in a uniform or did you not exclude the possibility that there might have been someone in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite. I did not see any military there, but I also allowed the possibility for a citizen wearing a uniform could have passed by. I did not see that, I did not register it. I simply allow for that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You allow for the possibility, but you did not tell Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Court that you saw someone in a uniform, but you will not exclude that there might have been one person; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to refresh your memory, and briefly, if you know: When did you see a unit which you called Kulin Ban.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. As a policeman, you said that you went around Sarajevo every day, that you travelled around Sarajevo every day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, if the nature of my assignment required that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And so when you discharged your duties, you had the possibility of frequently passing in the vicinity of the Rade Koncara Square or the other square which was nearby?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the war, outside my work, I didn't go to any of these squares unless on my way home or back, because one had to take care of one's own life. So I never used any free time to go around except when I had to do some shopping for the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But I'm speaking not about your leisure time; I'm speaking about your time on duty.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would come to -- yes, I did that, in those cases when I conducted investigations. And when did I have to do with this square when this incident happened, that is, when I went in there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... next question. I hear that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I do understand. Sorry [Interpretation] Thank you. My apologies to the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how many times and with what frequency, more or less, did you go to that area, to Alipasino Polje, during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Alipasino, I could have gone there on about ten occasions during the war, and it was always related to my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd now like the witness to confirm to us that he never saw, with his own eyes, military equipment or military premises in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interests of accuracy, since Mr. Piletta-Zanin has referred to two locations - that is, Rade Koncara Square and the broader area of Alipasino Polje - could he please clarify for the witness if he's now asking if he ever saw military premises in Alipasino Polje during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I shall do so gladly, reminding you that you yourself quoted precisely a moment ago what the witness had testified about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question, Witness, has to do with the two squares that we are talking about, and my second question, the Alipasino Polje area.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Alipasino Polje" is a very broad term. It encompasses a large part of the city.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters should kindly like to request the Chamber to note that the interpreters and the court reporters cannot do their job properly if there are several simultaneous speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the English booth asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, I do understand. I'm very sorry for that. I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are even speaking simultaneously, which is a great problem for the interpreters, so would you please pause. And may I ask Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear that the French booth is having the same problems. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not want to create any coalitions against me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, so will you please start your answer with telling us about the two squares. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I -- no, sorry. Did I see any military formation or its base on one of these two squares? Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Very precisely. You already gave us "no" to that question, but will you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for this explanation. Now, Witness, will you tell us if, in the area around these two squares, there were any military facilities, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to show two documents to the witness. It is two documents about which I have just communicated, which we were supplied by the Prosecution, and more precisely, from the binder that I referred to this morning. Their numbers are as follows, I mean their ERN numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... able to see it. And do you have copies for the booth?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As an exception, which has become a rule, yes, I did so. May I ask the usher to take them? May I ask for the ERN number for the transcript? Yes, thank you. So we have the document, which is 02056300, and then we have the second one, 02056280.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, just for the sake of practical -- you're going to tender these documents in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're required to prenumber them, and of course once they have got your Defence Exhibit number, everyone will be able to read what ERN numbers they are in and we'll be able to read it as well if they're on our desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be done as of the next week.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D54 and D55.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be precise, Mr. President, that with regard to the first document which we shall be producing, the handwritten additions were made in this document, but it seems that the original of the document also has these additions here, that is, that they were done by the person who was doing the documents. These additions were not made by the Defence. And I would like to add that we made some ten copies and that three copies were given to the booths, so that I reserved seven copies. Mr. President, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just wait until the Chamber has received the copies as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D54 is the document with last digits in the ERN 300. D55 is the document with the last three digits of the ERN number 280. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. And would you please, whenever you confront the witness with any part of it, first indicate to us, although we cannot read it, which part we're dealing with and then ask the interpreters to translate the specific part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. I will do so. I'm talking about the first document now, which is D54. We shall show the document to the witness, and we'll go to item 2 on the first page of the document. That is why we have not -- why we did not translate, Mr. President, anything except this item 2. I believe that you have this translation, but I must repeat that it was an improvisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please read aloud item 2 of the document that you have before you and which, on the left-hand side, has in handwriting "STRPOV," and so on, that is, "strictly confidential." "STRPOV" has in this upper left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the interpretation of this abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, will you please read first which is -- who is the sender of the document. Can you please read it out.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this has anything to do with an incident that I investigated, and I see no reason for me to read this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, the Defence has the right to ask you questions also if it's outside the scope of what you told the Court about your investigations if it is relevant for the case and if you would have any knowledge of it, so would you please answer the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin. On the other hand, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if this document is not known to the witness, I don't know whether there would be any problem if you'd say, "Could you agree that this document comes from --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, Witness, you agree with me that this was -- that this document was signed by a commander who is called Mustafa Dzebo. This is what I see on page 2. Yes or no, please. We shall save time in this way.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was he -- did he sign it? I don't know. But what is typed here is Mustafa Dzebo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that that's the answer you could expect under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I fully agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this a document you understand the witness has seen before or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, but you assume he had seen it before or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'd like only this witness, without wasting any more time, I want this witness to read item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- aloud and with proper pronunciation, and that is all I want him to do.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd do it if there was any mention of the Rade Koncara Square and the Zavnobih Square. I said a moment ago that Alipasino Polje is a very large area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are sorry. There were again several simultaneous speakers. Interpreters and court reporters cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This time I used my priority button. If we all speak at the same time, no one will know what words have been spoken by anyone else, so I urge to everyone that we wait not only until either the witness or counsel has finished what he wanted to say, but also to wait until the translation has been made. Mr. Kucanin, you don't have to worry about what could happen to you. The only thing Mr. Piletta-Zanin is asking you, to read the number 2, and we'll later find out what the relevance is. Would you please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why can't then Ms. Pilipovic read it. But I will do so, even though this is a military -- this is an army document and I just don't want that it turns out that I have to do something with the army or something. But I'll read it: [As interpreted] "To raise to the highest degree of alertness, to raise to the highest degree the alertness of the observers and observation points Brijesce Brdo 2, the MTB Alipasino Polje 3 MTB, the Hostel of Nuns 1 MTB, and other observation points set up at the level of battalions and companies."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In order not to waste any more time, Madam Pilipovic will actually read the other document. However, at this point I should like to ask the witness whether he can agree with me that there was at the Alipasino Polje battalion number 3 of the Motorised Brigade, that this battalion was located at the Alipasino Polje, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't agree. I can tell you about anything that I saw. You can ask me about any barracks inside the town, but if you ask me to agree that there were there, at Alipasino Polje, and I myself didn't see them, there's no way I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I merely asked you whether this document indicates the presence of the 3rd Battalion at Alipasino Polje; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you showed a document to a witness which seems to indicate clearly what you'd like the witness to confirm. The witness has answered that he cannot confirm, from his own knowledge, that the military presence, as stated in this document, was there. So I don't think you could repeat that question and ask him more or less, almost force him to tell us anything that he's not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. President. Very well. I will move on to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please have a look at the second document. My co-counsel, Madam Pilipovic, will read the relevant passages for the booths, and I should like to ask you to follow the reading of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you have in front of you a document emanating from the command of the 102nd Motorised Brigade, number 02/4-22?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you read on the document under item 1, communication centres?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Item 2, on command post of the 102nd Motorised Brigade in Alipasino Polje continuously operating in connection with PTT Sarajevo and the communication centre of the main staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Is that what you can read on the document?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Point 4: "On command post of the 1st Motorised Brigade in Alipasino Polje area operating in connection with PTT Sarajevo and the station communication centre of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Can you read this under item 4?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In the last line, under point number 2,: "The command post of the logistics battalion in Alipasino Polje area continuously operating in connection with PTT Sarajevo and the station communication centre of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Can you read this on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a portion that is handwritten here on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. We indicated that the handwritten notes were made by the author of the document, and the Court will be able to judge the authenticity of the document. All I want you to tell me now is whether you can read this on the document.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for my co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd be grateful if my friend could indicate where those read passages were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to make it short, I see the last page. I have two pages in English. On the last page it starts in the left upper top, commander 102 [indiscernible]. Do you have that, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Am I right in my understanding, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that there has been read from that page those parts which appear under [indiscernible], the relevant parts?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Mr. President. The items that have been read aloud are passages concerning Alipasino Polje. That is how on page 1, in the second item, in the second point, you have this mention of Alipasino Polje, and another one, and then the last one, which is not perhaps fully legible, and there was one more which is somewhere in the middle of the text, but I think we'll be able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fourth one, the fourth item.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to me at this stage, Mr. President, but I don't want to take up cross-examination time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I just make note of your answers in connection with this document. Would you now be so kind and tell us whether Rade Koncara Square was, according to your knowledge, divided in three stages, three locations, A, B, and C?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, yes, it is. Alipasino Polje is divided in so-called phases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether every one of these phases, A, B, and C, had some kind of police premises, including also those of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that every one of them had. However, we had call signs in various areas of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, let me now ask you whether your team took photographs on the occasion of these two shelling incidents on Rade Koncara Square and the other one. Did you always take photographs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did. That was their duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you no longer know for sure whether the photographs were taken in respect of both squares?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about various duties during the on-site investigation, and I mentioned the fact that all traces had to be sketched, marked, and photographed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude that photographs were taken in respect of both squares?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order not to waste time, my colleague, Madam Pilipovic, will present the photographs, the famous black boxes, and I will now move on to another incident. Let me just confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I should like you to now focus on the incident which happened on the 20th of July, 1993. First of all, I should like to know what you were doing during the period between the 20th and the 28th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly what I was doing during that period of time. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that each time there was an incident of this kind, your team would quickly move on to the scene of the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were fatalities, yes, if you're referring to my team of the public security centre, yes. If we were properly and promptly informed of the incident, yes, that would always be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, speaking of the incident that I just mentioned, that is, the one which occurred on the 20th of July, 1993, I should like to know why the report was made only eight days later.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day before yesterday I think I spoke about the fact that it was the citizens from this neighbourhood of Sarajevo had reported to us that there was frequent firing on their neighbourhood, and they believed that the firing position was a Serb house which was located some hundred metres away from them. And of course they requested protection from the police. In order to verify the authenticity of their claims, we selected two of our best ballistics experts --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Witness, but my question is as follows: You told us that whenever there was an incident of this kind, that is, involving fatalities, you would intervene right away. In this particular case, you intervened almost ten days later. Why this delay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, why the report was made only eight days later, and that's a different question from whether the witness intervened eight days later. Both questions are perfectly right, as far as I'm concerned, but they are different questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your remark, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, why was this report made eight or nine days later, that is, eight or nine days after the event, in view of what you stated, that is, that you would always intervene immediately in cases where an incident involved fatalities?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I also stated, I also added: If we had been promptly informed of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude from your answer that you were not promptly and timely informed of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The moment we received appropriate information, we visited the scene of the incident. I was about to explain to you how it happened, but you interrupted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm really very sorry for having interrupted you. You arrived, therefore, at the scene of the incident nine days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The only reason being that the neighbours failed to inform you of the incident earlier on?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because no one informed the police station, the relevant police station, of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So that was the only reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for being clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to show the witness another document, D56. The document is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I have it in front of me. Mr. President, we are still talking about the same type of activity, but this time it involves UNPROFOR forces. The document contains page 583 and it relates to the 13th of July, 1993. It was a Tuesday. I don't think I've had the opportunity of giving the document to the booths. I don't know whether they have it. If not, we can perhaps put it on the ELMO so that -- in order to avoid problems with interpretation. Mr. President, there are seven copies. I believe they will be distributed in a moment. There are enough copies. I suppose I can continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you have a report in front of you. Would you please focus on the interpretation, what I'm now going to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read page 2, Mr. President, item B, which bears the title "Local reported events." We have a number here, 2225, and the text goes as follows: "[In English] Alija Izetbegovic appealed for international help in a letter to UN Security General Boutros Boutros Ghali and other officials -- I think there's a quote in the text. I'm indicating for the record: "[In English] That the Serbian forces plan a general attack on the town itself--" I'm quoting in the text, and I think the word that follows is "said," "said Mr. Izetbegovic." And the quote of Mr. Izetbegovic goes on: "[In English] And stop this act of aggression" the word that comes after is probably "he," "he said." "[In English] Seemed to be designed to increase pressure on ABiH to accept ethnic partitioning." [Interpretation] Waiting for the end of the interpretation. Witness, as far as you can remember, is it not correct that during this period of time, intense attacks were being conducted around and at the city?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot help you with that. I'd love to, but I'm not sure. I don't want to make any guessings. As for the time period that you indicated, there is really nothing that I can state with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, isn't it true that during the night between the 21st and the 22nd -- I'm sorry, between the 20th and the 21st, violent combats occurred between the parties, and isn't it correct that Bosniak forces regained territory during that night?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't be of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to read this from the document, because we will lose too much time, however, I wish to state for the record that, under 2226, UN observers reported night attacks by BH troops, the attacks which happened precisely during the night when the incidents that we have been talking about occurred. Mr. President, I should like to tender this document. This would be D57, I think. That is, I would like to tender another document, D57, I believe, that is, page 592 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me just ask you: Just for the sake of the record, you indicated some facts which seem to be in this document. Were you referring to 2226, which starts with: "Outside Sarajevo, the Serb attack on Mount Igman, overlooking the city and UN controlled airport was reportedly amongst the fiercest in the area"? Is that the part you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. I was referring to the end of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the end of the paragraph also deals with Mount Igman. Is that the part that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the document does not bear an ERN number, at least the version that I have. My friend says that he wishes to tender it. He's asked the witness some questions in relation to it. I'd be grateful if my friend could indicate if this document came from the Prosecution, and if so, what the ERN number is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very pertinent question indeed, Mr. Ierace, but all I can tell you is that it is the same type of document as the ones that were previously produced by yourself and that you yourself accepted. You told us that there are certain difficulties with the ERN numbers. Sometimes there's only one, sometimes two, sometimes even three ERN numbers. So I don't think I'm able to answer your question at this point, but I don't think that it is as important as what this document may prove.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, a simple indication as to whether or not it came from the Prosecution would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond to that question as soon as I'm able to, as soon as I'm perfectly sure about what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps if you'd try to do this during the break, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. It very much appears to be an annex to the report of the committee of experts, so if that would be of any assistance. Another thing I'd like to ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin: You said, "But I don't think that it is as important as what this document may prove." I have still some problems. You're presenting a document, you ask a question to a witness who says, "I don't know anything about it," then you quote a few lines and you leave out that it is outside Sarajevo on Mount Igman. Well, that's what it says, at least, at the beginning. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not only that, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just wondering: I've got no problem in accepting that this might be true or not true, but what's the relation with the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have this other document which will be produced shortly, and you will be able to see that the combats which were defined by President Alija Izetbegovic as an overall attack against the town, an overall attack --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not mind if you want to prove this, but I do not see the relation with the testimony of this witness. I will be quite --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- accept to hear whatever as in evidence on this document by a witness you'll present in this case. You're perfectly entitled to do so. But what, as a matter of fact, happens, more or less now, is that you present a document to a witness who says, "I do not know anything about what is in this document. I don't know the document and I cannot confirm, neither deny, because I don't know it." And you present this as evidence, which is, at least, not very usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this witness testified that he was not at the scene of the incident shortly after the incident, just because he had not been promptly informed of the incident. I am stating some other potential reasons for that, and he told me that that was the only reason. We wish to prove that during that night, between the 20th and 21st, there were intense combats, so intense that President Izetbegovic appealed to the International Community. We would have understood it if mention had been made of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you say if the witness cannot testify on a certain document, since he doesn't know anything about it, then -- this is something the Chamber has to consider, whether you then tender that document into evidence not to prove that this is a document the witness doesn't know anything about, but from the content of what is in that document. That's your -- now I understand you better what -- why you want to tender this in evidence and why you want to have this put in evidence. That's proof of the -- that the events described in this document, although the witness doesn't know -- has testified that he doesn't know anything about these, are events that took place. At least that's perfectly --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's 10.30. We'll have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do apologise for resuming late. It had also to do with that we'd like to consider part of the issue I raised at the end of the session that ended at 10.30. There's no reason at this moment to come back to it, but please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will change the channel so as to be on the same channel with the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to go back to what we were talking about a moment ago. To your knowledge, during the period between the 20th and the 28th of July, 1993, would it be correct to say that there was considerable fighting in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you therefore cannot say either if the fighting went on during the night as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You ask me a question to which I have no answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. You went to investigate nine days after the event. Do you know if during that period anyone could touch this or that indication, trace?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. It was eight days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And therefore, would you agree with me when I say that if various traces could be interfered with, then the ballistic conclusions that you performed may not be all that correct, all that precise?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the bullet which was fired from an arm we found deep in the couch, and on the basis of that we could establish directly the direction from which the bullet had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of the existence of a building in that area which was called Zetra?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why, Witness, do you say "of course" that I was?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? Because Zetra was one of the symbols of the city of Sarajevo which the enemies generously destroyed and razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And who was in Zetra? I apologise. What was in Zetra?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able for tell you. All I know is that Zetra was a sports facility, that it contained a sports hall. What else was there, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know if Zetra was used as an army depot?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you were a policeman. Does the word "kazan" tell you something? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is part of the investigation that I did, I can talk about that, but as for the kazani, I cannot really. I don't know if that is part of the investigation. I can talk about that at length, if you like, but not today. On some other occasion, I shall be ready to do so. And please, do not forget that I was a professional who performed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kucanin, what questions will be put to you is first decided by the Defence. If there's any reason not to allow a question to be put to you, either the Prosecution will object or the Court will intervene. But the question just was whether the word "kazan" did mean anything to you, so if it is so, please tell us. If not, you don't have to tell us a lot unless you're asked to do so. But the question was just whether the word "kazan" does ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I'm merely afraid that it will provoke a debate, and I am not quite ready to do it. Perhaps if I say something that is not quite right, perhaps. But kazan, yes, it does tell me something. It is a vessel and it is also a part of Sarajevo in the streets on Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Don't worry. There's no need for any debate. If you'd just answer the questions, that's good enough. If you're not sure about what is the correct answer, just indicate that you either don't know or you're not sure or that you're sure as far as your answer is concerned. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Just to clarify the transcript, the word is kazani, but we are talking about the same thing. Mr. President, before I give the floor to Ms. Pilipovic, I'd like to produce and tender into evidence two documents which are of the same nature as those that we've already seen. These are documents 591 and 592, and they have to do with the day of the 27th of July, 1993. If we tender these -- if we are tendering these, it is because the fighting that we were talking about lasted until that time, and it seems that it was only after that that the police could produce their report. And it is for this reason that we wish to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let me be quite clear on this issue. You are producing documents, when you tender them into evidence, documents of which we still do not know the source, but I have some feeling that they might be annexes to the report of the Committee of Experts, which relate to fighting or at least combat activities in different areas, but that's for sure during that period of time. The Chamber has no difficulties in accepting these documents, but you should keep clearly in mind that whenever you are suggesting that these documents are clear evidence of another reason than the reason given by the witness for arriving only one week after the incident, at the spot of the incident, of course that's not the probative -- the potential probative value of these documents. You could imagine a lot of other explanations for that. I'm not going to guess on that. These documents indicate that at the places mentioned in these documents, according to those who did the investigations, on request of the Committee of Experts, if these are the Committee of Experts annexes, that they establish that there was heavy combat activities at these periods of time. We are not in a specific common-law court; we are in a mixed court. So therefore, the rules of admitting evidence might be a bit different from what our common-law friends are used to. But I'd just like to explain to you that admitting these documents into evidence means that this Court will consider these documents, at least if there's no other objections, of which I did not hear, that we'll consider these documents to see what probative value they have and we'll then, of course, look to the content of the document, and whatever suggestions you make on what kind of explanations it could give, well, of course we'll consider everything, but we'll first concentrate on the content of the documents, but I now see that there are no explicit explanations for another reason that the investigators came only after one week on the spot of the incident. So with this explanation from the Chamber, and looking at Mr. Ierace, he doesn't seem to object, but we are willing to admit these documents in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do object, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- the course we have taken so far is to consider objections after the witness has left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but since the point came up --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's the reason I haven't said anything at this stage, and I'm very mindful of the fact that the witness is very anxious to get away, and I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we first continue and deal with it at a later stage. But so then we know that you are going to tender these documents into evidence. If they could be distributed and if Ms. Pilipovic could continue the cross-examination right away while the usher is doing his distribution. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kucanin.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, and I believe you already confirmed that on the 10th and the 12th of November, and I believe you confirmed this, you gave a statement to the OTP investigators.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were asked, when you gave them your particulars, did you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters asked to make a pause. I do appreciate your willingness to finish the cross-examination as soon as possible, but the translators also have to do their work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in your statement that you gave, say that you were a policeman and then, in brackets, criminal inspector? You are not getting the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of education you have?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I completed all the schooling that was necessary for that particular job.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which job? The job of a policeman or a criminal inspector?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm an inspector -- a general criminal inspector. That is my title.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What does -- what kind of education, what kind of training, does one have to undergo to obtain that title?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any school -- what do you call it? Specialisation. What do you call it? It is only now that there is a faculty of criminal law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But can you tell us what kind of schools did you complete to obtain the rank of a criminal inspector?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general criminal inspector?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I completed a higher school and a special course for the general criminal inspector in general crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you became a criminal inspector on the basis of a course that you attended; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did this course take?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I attended seven or eight such courses, and this one lasted six months -- six or seven months.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When? When I say "when," I mean what year did you attend and complete this specialised course?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the general crime investigation, I believe it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kucanin, you told us that you performed the on-site investigation on Zavnobih Square; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notify the relevant investigating magistrate about this investigation?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I conducted this investigation, I think we could not do so or had he empowered us, now, after all this time, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But does one have to, when performing such investigations -- is the presence of the investigating magistrate necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he should be there, but there is an article, there is a provision which says that in the absence of a judge, then the competent person from the Ministry of the Interior, from the police, does it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are not sure if you notified the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, that either we could not look at him, so he was not present, or he was busy elsewhere and therefore empowered me to perform this investigation. But whatever was necessary to be done in terms of the investigation was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you tell us who was the ballistics expert in your team? I'm referring to what you said earlier, that you always had a ballistics expert along. Now, who was the ballistics expert that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. Can the Chamber please help me? Am I allowed to mention any names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you know the name of the ballistic expert that assisted you, you can tell the Court, yes. A.(redacted).

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long had (redacted) worked with you as a ballistics expert, I mean in your department?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are the criminal technology department. They are not part of us. But on various occasions we did investigations together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "on various occasions," you did investigations together, does that mean that prior to this incident which happened on the 9th of November, you had already performed on-site investigations with

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that prior to the 9th of November? Was it September, October?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, come. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But in any event, you said that it was before the event which happened on the 9th of November.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we had worked together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I seek a redaction of the transcript in relation to the name mentioned by the witness. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go into private session so I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so. Madam Registrar, could you please -- yes, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session again. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the individual that you described as ballistics expert, was he with you at both on-site investigations, both at the Zavnobih Square and Rade Koncara Square?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you made a report, the investigation report, in respect of both incidents, Zavnobih Square and Rade Koncara Square incidents.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have, because I was conducting the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, according to you, the person whom you described as ballistics expert, was he a well-experienced professional who could act as ballistics expert in this incident?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All crime technicians, including the individual you mentioned, had completed appropriate courses and training in order to be able to perform this work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are now telling us that all members of your team had merely completed courses that were necessary for the proper conduct of this type of work.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to crime technicians. They all completed specialised courses in addition to their normal educational background. I don't know exactly what kind of degrees they have, but they all went through additional appropriate courses where they were trained to perform their job in war circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of school is necessary for an individual to receive the title of a ballistics expert? Is a simple course sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kucanin, could you confirm for us that a member of your team took photographs of the site, both at Zavnobih Square and Rade Koncara Square?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that was his duty. Now, I cannot remember at this point whether I actually saw him take photographs, but that was his job. He should have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the report that you made on the 10th of November, 1993 concerning the event which had taken place on the 9th of November, 1993, the report that you yourself signed - and with the permission of the Chamber, perhaps I could give it to you, since I want to put to you one portion of the report and ask you whether what it contains is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I also have a copy of the report from my colleague, but I should like first the witness to identify the report and then to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it the original report in B/C/S, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original, Your Honour, is in B/C/S, but I have the English version as well. I have supplied the interpreters with both versions. However, with your permission, I would like to read only a portion of the text which can be found on page 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is this the report that you made concerning the incident of the 9th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be sure, Ms. Pilipovic, is this the same document as Exhibit 1840?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's already distributed. That could have been shown to the witness and that would have saved us three minutes of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note that there is a redaction to be made from that exhibit, and if at some point they could be returned and that redaction will be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or would you prefer to have it admitted under seal, which is also a possibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd prefer that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you then please give the original exhibit. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, Witness, of the document that is now in front of you, there is a text that I am now going to read, the one starting with the word "the tail."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us that these are the contents of your report: "The tail section of the shell was not found because members of the army had taken it away. But according to eyewitness statements and the assessment of the crime technician, it was a 120-millimetre shell fired from the direction of Nedzarici." Did you write this in your report?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD KUCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
